caseStudy.title: Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments
caseStudy.summary: Category 2 (semi-urgent) patients referred by their GP to Riverside's specialist outpatient clinics wait an average 74 days from referral receipt to first appointment (illustrative). Referrals arrive by fax, post and e-referral, sit in clinic inboxes awaiting registration and a weekly consultant triage session, and 28% are returned to the GP as incomplete. Patients and GPs chase status through the outpatient call centre ('where is my referral' is 34% of calls). Target: referral-to-first-appointment 74 days → ≤45 days within 12 months; referral-status calls down 40%; urgency-upgrade rate at first appointment must not rise. Recommendation: Option B — buy an e-referral and triage platform and integrate it with the patient administration system (PAS) via a FHIR integration engine. Phased: e-referral and validation MVP in two pilot clinics, then daily protocol-led triage and SMS booking offers, then network-wide roll-out. Key insight: the biggest leak wasn't clinic capacity — it was referrals waiting in inboxes for a weekly triage session. Re-framing triage as a daily, protocol-led task with consultant oversight of exceptions is what unlocked the outcome.
caseStudy.disclaimer: Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

participant.overview:
This first session launches the initiative you will carry through all twelve sessions. You'll bring a real problem from your workplace (sanitised), and by 21:00 you'll have a one-page Discovery Brief and a first-cut Stakeholder Register, both drafted with your AI agent and reviewed by you.

We use Playbook 01 Steps 1 and 2. The AI is very good at restating messy narratives in plain language, proposing assumptions and listing stakeholder groups you forgot. It is very bad at knowing who actually holds the decision rights in your organisation, so that's the part you own.

Throughout the course the instructor works one initiative live: *Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments*, an illustrative scenario at Riverside Health Network, a fictional public health service. No real patient data is used. You'll see each artefact built on that case before you build yours.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**Bad Discovery looks for requirements. Good Discovery looks for decisions.** Most projects don't fail at delivery — they fail because the wrong decisions were made early, by the wrong people.

- Capture the decisions that must be made — and who owns each one.
- Map stakeholders by the decisions they control, not the org chart.
- If a stakeholder can't name a decision they own, they're not the right stakeholder.

**The questions that matter:** Who is actually accountable? What decision are we really making? What does success look like for each person — in their words?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** Sponsor 1:1, stakeholder interviews, org-chart vs decision-rights mapping, document review (strategy, prior business cases).

sections.heading: Playbook 01 · Step 1 — Frame the Problem
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Initiative Brief or Problem Statement

**What to do**
- Restate the problem in one sentence using plain business language
- Identify the measurable outcome the business is seeking
- Capture three working assumptions and three open questions
- Avoid solutions or technology choices at this stage

**Success criteria**
- Problem statement is one sentence and is outcome-focused
- Assumptions and open questions are explicit
- No solution language has crept in

**Produce:** Problem Statement (one sentence); Target Outcome; Assumptions (3); Open Questions (3)

**Step output:** Discovery Brief (one page)

sections.heading: Playbook 01 · Step 2 — Identify Stakeholders
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Sponsor and Initial Stakeholder List, Discovery Brief

**What to do**
- List every stakeholder group affected, internal and external
- Capture role, decision rights, and what success looks like for each
- Identify who owns each in-scope process or system
- Flag stakeholders likely to block, slow, or accelerate the work

**Success criteria**
- All decision-makers are named, not just titles
- Each stakeholder has a stated success measure
- Blockers and accelerators are explicitly flagged

**Produce:** Name; Role; Group; Decision Rights; What Success Looks Like; Risk Flag (Blocker / Neutral / Accelerator)

**Step output:** Stakeholder Register

sections.heading: Setting up your agent for the whole course
sections.body:
You will use one AI workspace for all twelve sessions, so set it up properly tonight.

| Tool | Where | What to load |
|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT | Projects (or a Custom GPT) | Paste the playbook prompt as instructions; upload your sanitised brief as a file |
| Gemini | Gems → New Gem | Playbook as instructions; attach up to 10 files or a Drive folder |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot | Agent Builder / Copilot Studio | Playbook as instructions; ground on a SharePoint folder |

Name it after your initiative (e.g. *Outpatient Access BA Agent*). Every week you'll add the previous artefact to its knowledge, so the chain builds itself: Decision Register → To-Be Map → Fix List → Story Backlog → Business Case → Benefits Plan.

The operating pattern never changes: **set the role and paste the playbook → feed your inputs → run one step → review against the success criteria → flag gaps, don't invent → carry the output forward.**

**Try it in another industry.** *Fintech:* "We need a new onboarding app" — rewrite it as the outcome (e.g. what share of applicants abandon at the AML/KYC identity check, and the target). *Blockchain:* "Let's put supplier credentials on-chain" — which decision would that actually change, and who owns it?

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. Health information is sensitive information: never paste patient names, URNs, Medicare numbers, dates of birth, referral letters or clinical notes into any AI tool your organisation hasn't approved for it. The agent drafts; you own the decision.

sections.heading: Worked example — Outpatient access
sections.body:
*Instructor demo initiative: Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments (Riverside Health Network). Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation. No real patient data is used.*

**Discovery Brief (one page).** Problem: Category 2 (semi-urgent) patients wait an average 74 days from referral receipt to first specialist outpatient appointment; 34% of calls to the outpatient call centre are ‘where is my referral’. Target outcome: ≤45 days within 12 months, with no rise in the urgency-upgrade rate at first appointment. Assumptions: consultants remain clinically accountable for triage; clinic capacity is not the main constraint; routine referrals can be matched to approved triage protocols from the information GPs already send. Open questions: what share of referrals is genuinely protocol-matchable? which mandatory fields or results are most often missing? which clinic runs the fastest current triage, and why?

**Stakeholder Register.** Executive Director Ambulatory Care — sponsor; approves any service standard or process change; success = shorter waits and fewer complaints; Accelerator. Director of Medical Services — chairs clinical governance and owns triage protocol approval; Neutral until safety controls are clear. Chief Digital Health Officer (CDHO) — owns the referral channel and PAS integration decision; Accelerator. Heads of Unit (e.g. cardiology, orthopaedics) — own clinic templates and triage rules; Blocker if consulted late, Accelerator if engaged early. Privacy Officer — advises on Privacy Act and state health records obligations; Neutral. Outpatient admin team and nursing/ANMF representatives — affected by new roles; Blocker if consulted late. GPs via the local Primary Health Network (PHN) liaison — affected by e-referral changes; Neutral. Consumer advisory group — patient voice; Accelerator.

A.heading: Is this a build problem?
A.body:
Pathway A suits a problem that needs **a new tool**, not a better process inside existing ones. The reference build is one BA plus Claude, no engineering team, shipping a live platform with nine role types.

**Test your problem:**
- Does solving it need screens, data and users that don't exist today?
- Can you name who would *use* it and who would *accept* each release?
- Is there no build team, or a long queue for one?

The BA's job on this pathway is the **specification of record**: every change begins as a story with acceptance criteria that the builder reads live. Ambiguity doesn't become a question; it becomes wrong code.
A.example: Riverside: a referral status page for GPs and patients is a build problem; triage rules are not.

B.heading: Where does your BA time go?
B.body:
Pathway B automates **the BA role itself**. Before you pick agents, find where your hours go across the lifecycle: Discover, Clarify, Define, Validate, Deliver, Improve.

**Typical sinks:** writing up meeting notes and actions, chasing decisions, rewriting vague requirements, drafting AC, checking stories against standards, keeping RAID current.

The Rovo BA pack has around 20 automations, but nobody builds 20. You'll pick the three that save the most time on your initiative, build them, and measure them.
B.example: Riverside BA: ~6 hrs/week on meeting write-ups and RAID, ~4 on reworking stories that fail refinement.

C.heading: Where does work wait between roles?
C.body:
Pathway C automates **a theme across roles**, such as delivery: requirements → solution → stories → test → docs. The value isn't faster drafting; it's removing the waits and rework *between* people.

The four handoff failures: **lost context**, **broken traceability**, **late rework** (gaps found in testing, not analysis) and **ungoverned AI** (fast drafts with no gates). Find which ones hurt your initiative.

The rule on this pathway is absolute: **agents never self-approve**. Only a human moves work out of review.
C.example: Riverside: requirements wait 2 weeks for design review; 30% of test defects trace to missing AC.

sections.heading: Playbook 01 · Step 3 — Map Influence and Interest
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Stakeholder Register

**What to do**
- Plot each stakeholder on a 2x2 of Influence (low/high) vs Interest (low/high)
- Identify the four to six stakeholders in the high/high quadrant — the keys
- Define an engagement cadence for each quadrant
- Note any stakeholder whose position is likely to shift over the initiative

**Success criteria**
- Every stakeholder is plotted
- Each quadrant has a defined engagement approach
- Position shifts are anticipated, not discovered late

**Produce:** Influence/Interest Matrix (with stakeholder names plotted); Quadrant Engagement Plan (quadrant -> cadence -> channel -> owner); Watchlist (stakeholders likely to shift quadrant)

**Step output:** Stakeholder Map

sections.heading: Playbook 01 · Step 4 — Surface the Real Decisions
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Discovery Brief, Stakeholder Map

**What to do**
- List every decision that must be made before delivery can begin
- For each decision, name the single accountable decision-maker
- Identify what information is needed to make the decision well
- Sequence the decisions in the order they need to happen

**Success criteria**
- Each decision has one accountable name, not a committee
- Information needs are concrete, not vague
- The sequence is logically ordered with dependencies called out

**Produce:** Decision; Accountable; Information Needed; Earliest Date Required; Depends On

**Step output:** Decision Register

sections.heading: Prompting AI as a challenger, not a scribe
sections.body:
The weakest use of AI in discovery is 'write me a stakeholder map'. The strongest is adversarial:

- *"Here is my Decision Register. Which decisions are implied by my open questions but missing?"*
- *"Which rows name a group rather than one accountable person? Rewrite them as a question I should ask the sponsor."*
- *"Play a sceptical CFO. Which decision would you insist on before funding discovery further?"*

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**Most process pain isn't in the tasks — it's in the handoffs.** Teams optimise tasks endlessly while value keeps leaking between roles and systems.

- Map the lanes, then count the handoffs and wait states.
- Quantify every pain point in time, cost and risk.
- Design the To-Be to remove handoffs — don't paper over them.

**The questions that matter:** Show me how it really works, not how the manual says. Where does it wait? Where does it come back? What do you do when it breaks?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** SME walkthroughs, 'follow the work' observation, system logs and volumes, a sample of real cases, a live process-mapping workshop.

sections.heading: Playbook 02 · Step 1 — Confirm Scope and Lanes
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Process Scope Statement

**What to do**
- Confirm the trigger event that starts the process and the outcome that ends it
- Identify the participating roles or systems (these become BPMN pool/lanes)
- Define what is explicitly out of scope to prevent map creep
- Agree the level of detail (L1 end-to-end, L2 per role, L3 task-level)

sections.heading: Playbook 02 · Step 2 — Map the As-Is
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Process Scope Confirmation, SME interviews

**What to do**
- Capture each task, gateway and event in BPMN 2.0 notation
- Place every task in the correct lane — never blur accountabilities
- Use exclusive (XOR) gateways for decisions, parallel (AND) for concurrent work
- Note volumes, average duration, and rework rate at each task where data exists

**Success criteria**
- BPMN is syntactically correct (one start, one end per pool, gateways balance)
- Every task sits in exactly one lane
- Operational data is captured where available, gaps are flagged

**Produce:** As-Is BPMN Diagram; Task Inventory (task -> lane -> duration -> volume -> notes); Data Gaps Log

**Step output:** As-Is Process Map

sections.heading: BPMN essentials you'll use
sections.body:
| Element | Meaning | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Start / end event (circle) | Trigger and outcome | Clock start and stop of your North Star later |
| Task (rounded box) | Work done by a role | One verb + noun: *Validate referral* |
| Exclusive gateway (X diamond) | Either/or decision | *Protocol match?* yes / no |
| Parallel gateway (+ diamond) | Both paths at once | Notify patient *and* start triage |
| Pool / lane | Who does it | One lane per role or system |
| Message flow (dashed) | Handoff between organisations | GP practice → Referral Hub |

Count handoffs (every lane crossing) and wait states (every time work sits in a queue). Those two numbers are your As-Is baseline for the acid test in the next session.

AI tip: ask for **Mermaid flowchart** or **BPMN XML** output, then paste it into Mermaid Live, draw.io or Camunda Modeler. Always check gateways: models frequently use exclusive gateways where the work is actually parallel.

**Try it in another industry.** *Insurance:* sketch the As-Is for a home-contents claim from first notice of loss to settlement and count the handoffs between call centre, assessor and fraud team. *Finance:* map month-end reporting from ledger close to board pack and count the wait states between business units and group finance.

**Model answers (worked example).** Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation. No real patient data.

**Process Scope Confirmation:** Trigger: a GP decides to refer a patient and sends a referral (fax, post or e-referral). End event: first specialist outpatient appointment attended. Lanes: Patient, GP practice, Referral Hub (admin), Specialist Clinic (triage clinician), Bookings. participant.bigIdea: Design the To-Be to remove handoffs; don't paper over them.
participant.overview:
Tonight you turn the As-Is into an improvement. First you name and quantify each pain point (wait, rework, manual-on-digital, handoff) in time, cost and risk. Then you design a To-Be that removes the biggest ones, and you prove it with the side-by-side acid test: cycle time, handoffs and automated steps, before and after.

AI is strong at generating redesign patterns (parallelise, validate at source, straight-through processing, eliminate the batch) and at doing the arithmetic. It is weak at knowing what's legally or politically possible, so every To-Be change needs a named control or a decision on the register.

Link every To-Be change to a control or a decision owner

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**Most process pain isn't in the tasks — it's in the handoffs.** Teams optimise tasks endlessly while value keeps leaking between roles and systems.

- Map the lanes, then count the handoffs and wait states.
- Quantify every pain point in time, cost and risk.
- Design the To-Be to remove handoffs — don't paper over them.

**The questions that matter:** Show me how it really works, not how the manual says. Where does it wait? Where does it come back? What do you do when it breaks?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** SME walkthroughs, 'follow the work' observation, system logs and volumes, a sample of real cases, a live process-mapping workshop.

sections.heading: Playbook 02 · Step 3 — Identify Pain Points and Value Leaks
sections.body:
**Inputs:** As-Is Process Map, Task Inventory

**What to do**
- Handoffs between lanes (each handoff is a candidate for delay or loss)
- Rework loops where work returns to an earlier task
- Manual tasks operating on structured digital data (automation candidates)
- Wait states between tasks that add no value

**Success criteria**
- Every handoff is named
- Rework loops are quantified, not just observed
- Pain points are categorised so they can be prioritised

**Produce:** Location (task or handoff); Type (handoff / rework / manual / wait); Impact (time, cost, risk, CX); Quantified Cost (where possible); Priority (H/M/L)

**Step output:** Pain Point Register

sections.heading: Playbook 02 · Step 4 — Design the To-Be
sections.body:
**Inputs:** As-Is Process Map, Pain Point Register

**What to do**
- Eliminate, automate, or simplify each high-priority pain point
- Reduce handoffs wherever a single role can own end-to-end
- Replace sequential steps with parallel where data allows
- Quantify the expected improvement against each As-Is metric

**Success criteria**
- Every high-priority pain point is addressed in the To-Be
- Improvements are quantified with explicit assumptions
- Change impact on roles is named, not glossed over

**Produce:** To-Be BPMN Diagram; Change Summary (As-Is task -> To-Be change -> expected impact); Role Impact Note (which roles change, by how much)

**Step output:** To-Be Process Map

sections.heading: Redesign patterns to ask AI for
sections.body:
| Pattern | Removes | Worked example |
|---|---|---|
| Capture at source | Inbox and re-keying waits | GP sends a structured e-referral straight into the triage queue; patient notified in parallel |
| Validate at entry | Rework loops | Mandatory fields and results checked at submission |
| Single data spine | Duplicate entry | One referral record shared e-referral ↔ PAS via FHIR |
| Kill the batch | Batch waits | Weekly posted booking letters → daily SMS offers |
| Straight-through + exceptions | Low-value touches | Protocol-matched routine referrals triaged daily by a nurse; exceptions to the consultant |

Ask the agent: *"For each pain point, propose two patterns, the control each would need, and which decision on my register it depends on."*

**Try it in another industry.** *Accounting:* apply 'validate at entry' and 'kill the batch' to expense claims that sit in a monthly approval run. *Professional Sports:* apply 'single data spine' to membership renewals where ticketing, CRM and the club app each hold a different member record.

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. Health information is sensitive information: never paste patient names, URNs, Medicare numbers, dates of birth, referral letters or clinical notes into any AI tool your organisation hasn't approved for it. The agent drafts; you own the decision.

sections.heading: Worked example — Outpatient access
sections.body:
*Instructor demo initiative: Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments (Riverside Health Network). Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation. No real patient data is used.*

**Pain Point Register.** P1 Inbox and weekly-triage delay — wait — up to 21 days, ~$1.1m/yr in status calls, avoidable ED presentations while waiting and duplicate re-referrals (illustrative). P2 Incomplete referrals returned to the GP — rework loop — 28% of referrals, ~$640k/yr. P3 Manual re-keying of fax/PDF referrals into the PAS — manual-on-digital — ~$380k/yr. P4 Weekly posted booking letters — wait — adds up to 7 days, ~$300k/yr including non-attendance from late letters.

**To-Be Process Map.** GP sends a structured e-referral straight into a daily triage queue; patient is notified by SMS in parallel (removes P1). Mandatory fields and results validated at submission with guided correction (removes P2’s loop). Single referral record shared e-referral ↔ PAS via FHIR (removes P3). Daily SMS appointment offers (removes P4). Protocol-matched routine referrals triaged daily by a clinical nurse consultant, exceptions routed to the consultant. Acid test: cycle time 74 → ≤45 days; handoffs 7 → 4; 2 of 5 steps automated; new controls: consultant audit sample of 10% of protocol-triaged referrals + urgency-upgrade watch.

A.body:
The build pathway removes handoffs by making **the spec the only copy**. The builder reads the story live; tests reference the story ID; release notes quote it. Change the story, and everything downstream follows.

Design rule: if a requirement exists in two places, one is wrong. Decide where the spec of record lives before anything is built.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**One North Star. Two tiers of drivers. No vanity metrics.** If your dashboard has fifty KPIs, your dashboard has zero KPIs.

- Pick one accountable metric with a real baseline and target.
- Decompose it into drivers an exec can read on one page.
- Convert each gap into a dollar value and rank the leaks.

**The questions that matter:** What does this field actually contain? Who owns it? Is this number trusted? What would 'good' look like here?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** Data profiling, report and dashboard review, pulling a sample extract, interviews with data owners, benchmark research.

**Success criteria**
- One metric is chosen, not three

- Decompose each Tier-1 driver into two or three Tier-2 operational metrics
- For every leaf metric, name the system that holds the data and the owner
- Keep the tree shallow enough that an exec can read it on one page

**Success criteria**
- The maths is sound: Tier-1 drivers reconstruct the North Star
- Every leaf metric has a named owner and data source
- The tree fits on a single page

sections.heading: Testing a metric definition with AI
sections.body:
Paste your definition and ask: *"Give me five ways two analysts could calculate this differently."* Typical gaps it finds: which timestamp starts the clock, calendar vs business days, how re-opened cases count, mean vs median, which population is excluded.

Then use a guardrail metric. A North Star pushed hard will distort behaviour; the worked example guards *referral-to-first-appointment* with an *urgency-upgrade rate must not rise* watch, a patient-safety guardrail owned by clinical governance.

**Working with data safely.** Ask the agent to generate a 200-row synthetic dataset with the same columns as your real extract, build your formulas on that, then run them yourself inside your organisation's environment. With health data this is non-negotiable: build on synthetic referrals, never on an extract containing patient details.

**Try it in another industry.** *Government & NGOs:* propose a North Star for a grants platform (days from application to funding decision) and its guardrail (audit findings must not rise). *Higher Education:* run the five-ways prompt on 'time to enrol' — census dates, part-time students and re-enrolments will all surface.

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. Health information is sensitive information: never paste patient names, URNs, Medicare numbers, dates of birth, referral letters or clinical notes into any AI tool your organisation hasn't approved for it. The agent drafts; you own the decision.

sections.heading: Worked example — Outpatient access
sections.body:
*Instructor demo initiative: Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments (Riverside Health Network). Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation. No real patient data is used.*

**North Star Metric Definition.** Metric: calendar days from referral receipt (first arrival in any Riverside channel) to first specialist outpatient appointment attended, Category 2 referrals. Baseline: 74 days (12-month average, illustrative). Target: ≤45 days within 12 months of R1 go-live. Owner: Executive Director Ambulatory Care. What it doesn’t measure: triage quality and clinical outcomes — guarded by an urgency-upgrade watch metric (referrals upgraded in urgency at first appointment) that must not rise.

**KPI Tree.** Tier-1 drivers: referral intake and triage lead time; booking lead time; clinic slot wait. Tier-2 (with owner + source): % referrals received as structured e-referrals (CDHO, e-referral analytics); % referrals complete at first submission (Outpatient Operations Manager, referral data mart); % routine referrals triaged under protocol within 2 days (Director of Medical Services, triage log); triage queue age p95 (Heads of Unit, PAS waitlist report); days triage→appointment booked (Bookings lead, PAS).

**Inputs:** KPI Tree, Available Data Sources

**What to do**
- For each leaf metric, plot the distribution and identify outliers
- Quantify the gap between current performance and a reasonable benchmark
- Convert each gap into a dollar value (revenue lost, cost incurred, risk carried)
- Rank leaks by dollar value and by ease of fixing

**Success criteria**
- Every leak has a dollar value with stated assumptions
- Outliers are investigated, not deleted
- The top three leaks are clearly the top three

**Inputs:** Value Leak Analysis

**What to do**
- Plot each leak on a 2x2 of Dollar Impact vs Ease of Fixing
- Pick the top three from the high-impact / high-ease quadrant
- For each pick, name the leading indicator that will move first if the fix works
- Define a check-in cadence to track movement against the leading indicator

**Success criteria**
- Three leaks are picked, not seven
- Each pick has a leading indicator separate from the lagging metric
- Cadence is realistic and owned

sections.heading: The value-leak formula
sections.body:
**Leak value per year = (current − benchmark) × affected volume × unit cost × 12**

Worked example (illustrative): incomplete referrals are returned to the GP at 28% against an 8% benchmark. On ~3,000 referrals a month, that's ~600 extra returned referrals monthly. At a blended rework cost of ~$89 each (re-registration, GP contact and clinician re-triage), that's ~$640k a year.

Ask AI: *"Check this calculation for unit errors and double counting with Leak 1. List every assumption I need to footnote."* Double counting is the most common error: call-centre demand often appears in two leaks.

**Try it in another industry.** *Law Enforcement:* value the leak when case files are returned for missing evidence-handling fields (gap × volume × officer hours). *Logistics:* value failed first-attempt deliveries against a best-practice rate — redelivery cost and customer contacts are classic double counts.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**A requirement that can't be tested can't be delivered.** Stories that fail INVEST become tech debt before they become code.

- Number every requirement and trace it to the To-Be.
- Slice into INVEST stories with real roles and outcomes.
- Write Given/When/Then for happy, alternative and failure paths.

**The questions that matter:** Give me a real example. What happens on the unhappy path? How would we know this works in test?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** Story-mapping workshop, example mapping (rules via examples), walking the To-Be with users, reviewing the prioritised fix list.

sections.heading: Playbook 04 · Step 1 — Capture Requirements
sections.body:
**Inputs:** To-Be Process Map, Prioritised Fix List, Solution Constraints

**What to do**
- Capture every functional requirement the To-Be implies, in plain language
- Capture non-functional requirements: performance, security, availability, accessibility, compliance
- Number every requirement so it can be traced through delivery and testing
- Tag each requirement with its source (which To-Be task or fix it comes from)

**Success criteria**
- Each requirement is a single statement, not a paragraph
- Functional and non-functional are clearly separated
- Every requirement traces back to a To-Be element

**Produce:** ID (REQ-001, REQ-002...); Type (Functional / Non-Functional); Statement; Source (To-Be task or fix); Priority (Must / Should / Could / Won't)

**Step output:** Requirements Catalogue

sections.heading: Playbook 04 · Step 2 — Slice into User Stories
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Requirements Catalogue

**What to do**
- Use the form: As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <outcome>
- Each story must be independent, valuable, and small enough for one sprint
- Group stories under epics that map to To-Be process areas
- Reject any story that is really a task, technical detail, or wish

**Success criteria**
- Every story has a real role, not 'user'
- Every story has a stated outcome, not a feature description
- Stories pass the INVEST check (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable)

**Produce:** Epic Map (epic -> stories); Story Backlog (ID, story, epic, priority, dependencies)

**Step output:** Story Backlog

sections.heading: INVEST and story slicing
sections.body:
| Letter | Test | Common AI failure |
|---|---|---|
| Independent | Can be built in any order | Stories chained to a 'setup' story |
| Negotiable | Describes the need, not the UI | 'Click the blue button' |
| Valuable | A real role gets a real outcome | 'As a system…' |
| Estimable | Team can size it | Vague verbs: 'manage', 'handle' |
| Small | Fits a sprint | Epics disguised as stories |
| Testable | Clear pass/fail | No measurable outcome |

Slice by workflow step, business rule, data variation or happy/unhappy path, never by technical layer. Ask the agent: *"Slice REQ-001 three different ways and tell me which slicing delivers value earliest."*

**Try it in another industry.** *Fintech:* write a story and NFRs for a BNPL hardship request — PCI DSS and responsible-lending rules become testable NFRs. *Higher Education:* slice 'students can manage their enrolment' by workflow step and by business rule (prerequisites, census date).

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. Health information is sensitive information: never paste patient names, URNs, Medicare numbers, dates of birth, referral letters or clinical notes into any AI tool your organisation hasn't approved for it. The agent drafts; you own the decision.

sections.heading: Worked example — Outpatient access
sections.body:
*Instructor demo initiative: Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments (Riverside Health Network). Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation. No real patient data is used.*

**Requirements Catalogue.** REQ-001 (Must): a GP can submit a structured e-referral from their practice software, with results attached — traces to To-Be step 1. REQ-004 (Must): the patient receives an SMS acknowledgement within 1 hour of referral acceptance — To-Be step 1. REQ-009 (Must): patient notices available in the 10 most-used community languages and accessible formats — NFR. REQ-014 (Must): mandatory fields and results are validated at submission with guided correction — To-Be step 2. NFRs: WCAG 2.2 AA, Privacy Act (APPs) and state health records compliance, HL7 FHIR interoperability with the PAS, audit log of every record access, 99.5% availability. All numbered, MoSCoW-prioritised and traced.

**Story Backlog.** “As a referring GP, I want to submit a complete e-referral with results attached, so that my patient enters triage without being returned for missing information.” AC — happy: Given all mandatory fields and results are attached, When I submit, Then I get a referral ID, the patient gets an SMS acknowledgement, and the clock starts. Alternative: Given a required result is missing, When validation fails, Then I’m shown exactly what is missing without losing my draft. Failure: Given the referral doesn’t match an approved triage protocol, When triage runs, Then it routes to the consultant queue and the expected triage date is visible to me. Passed INVEST.

participant.overview:
Tonight you make your stories testable and your scope defensible. You write Given/When/Then acceptance criteria for the happy, alternative and failure paths, then build a traceability matrix linking requirement → story → test case → To-Be step → decision. AI can generate unhappy paths you didn't think of and run the orphan check mechanically across a large table. You decide which edge cases matter and lock the MVP scope with the sponsor.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**A requirement that can't be tested can't be delivered.** Stories that fail INVEST become tech debt before they become code.

- Number every requirement and trace it to the To-Be.
- Slice into INVEST stories with real roles and outcomes.
- Write Given/When/Then for happy, alternative and failure paths.

**The questions that matter:** Give me a real example. What happens on the unhappy path? How would we know this works in test?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** Story-mapping workshop, example mapping (rules via examples), walking the To-Be with users, reviewing the prioritised fix list.

sections.heading: Playbook 04 · Step 3 — Write Acceptance Criteria
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Story Backlog

**What to do**
- Write acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then form
- Cover the happy path, the main alternative paths, and the failure modes
- Include criteria for non-functional requirements that apply to the story
- Confirm each criterion is testable without ambiguity

**Success criteria**
- Every story has at least one happy-path and one failure-path criterion
- Each criterion would produce an unambiguous pass/fail in test
- Non-functional aspects (timing, security) are not forgotten

**Produce:** Story ID; AC-1 (Given/When/Then) — happy path; AC-2 (Given/When/Then) — alternative path; AC-3 (Given/When/Then) — failure path; Non-Functional AC (if any)

**Step output:** Story Backlog with Acceptance Criteria

sections.heading: Playbook 04 · Step 4 — Build the Traceability Matrix
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Requirements Catalogue, Story Backlog with Acceptance Criteria

**What to do**
- Build a matrix linking each REQ to the stories that satisfy it
- Link each story to the test cases that will verify it
- Flag any REQ with no story (gap) and any story with no REQ (scope creep)
- Confirm the sponsor and tech lead both sign off the matrix

**Success criteria**
- No orphan requirements
- No orphan stories
- Sign-off is recorded with date and name

**Produce:** Traceability Matrix (REQ ID -> Story IDs -> Test Case IDs); Gap List (orphans in either direction); Sign-Off Record

**Step output:** Traceability Matrix

sections.heading: Given/When/Then that actually tests
sections.body:
Good AC is concrete and observable:

- **Given** all mandatory fields and results are attached, **When** the GP submits, **Then** a referral ID is shown, the patient receives an SMS acknowledgement within 1 hour and the clock starts.
- **Given** a required result is missing, **When** validation fails, **Then** the GP is shown exactly what is missing without losing the draft.
- **Given** the referral doesn't match an approved triage protocol, **When** triage runs, **Then** it routes to the consultant queue and the GP can see the expected triage date.

Ask the agent: *"List ten unhappy paths for this story ranked by likelihood × harm."* Keep the top three as AC; push the rest to test scenarios.

**Try it in another industry.** *Technology & Software:* write Given/When/Then for the opt-out path of an AI feature rollout. *Blockchain:* write the failure-path AC for a digital-identity credential that has been revoked — what exactly does the verifier see?

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. Health information is sensitive information: never paste patient names, URNs, Medicare numbers, dates of birth, referral letters or clinical notes into any AI tool your organisation hasn't approved for it. The agent drafts; you own the decision.

**Inputs:** Solution Options Matrix, Recommended Option

**What to do**

A.heading: Four decisions to cost
A.body:
The reference build names four decisions someone had to write down:

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**Delivery ships the solution. Change makes it stick.** Most change plans train people and forget Awareness, Desire and Reinforcement.

- Sequence releases that each deliver standalone value.
- Map change with ADKAR — skip a stage and adoption stalls.
- Diarise benefits reviews before go-live, not after.

**The questions that matter:** Who has to work differently, and do they know? What would make this not stick? How will we know the benefit actually landed?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** Change-readiness conversations, capacity/planning workshop, impact interviews with affected groups, baseline measurement before go-live.

sections.heading: Playbook 06 · Steps 1, 2, 3
sections.body:
### Playbook 06 · Step 1 — Sequence the Delivery Roadmap

**Inputs:** Approved Business Case, Story Backlog

**What to do**
- Group stories into releases that each deliver standalone value
- Sequence releases so dependencies are respected and risk is retired early
- Set a realistic target date for each release based on team capacity
- Identify the minimum viable release that can go live first

**Success criteria**
- Each release has a stated value, not just a feature list
- The first release is genuinely minimum viable
- The roadmap is honest about capacity, not aspirational

**Produce:** Delivery Roadmap (release -> stories -> target date -> value delivered); Dependency Map (technical and organisational); Minimum Viable Release Definition

**Step output:** Delivery Roadmap

---

### Playbook 06 · Step 2 — Run the Change Impact Assessment

**Inputs:** Delivery Roadmap, Change Impact Inputs

**What to do**
- Identify what specifically changes: process, system, role, performance measure
- Rate the change magnitude (small / moderate / significant / transformational)
- Identify what training, comms or support each group needs
- Identify groups whose performance measures must change to support the new way of working

**Success criteria**
- No affected group is missed
- Magnitude ratings are consistent across groups
- Performance measure changes are explicit, not implied

**Produce:** Group; What Changes; Magnitude; Training Needed; Comms Needed; Performance Measure Changes

**Step output:** Change Impact Assessment

---

### Playbook 06 · Step 3 — Build the Change Plan

**Inputs:** Change Impact Assessment, Delivery Roadmap

**What to do**
- Map interventions to the ADKAR stages (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement)
- Sequence interventions so they precede the technical release that needs them
- Identify change champions in each affected group
- Define adoption metrics that will be tracked through and after go-live

**Success criteria**
- Every ADKAR stage has at least one intervention
- Interventions are timed against the roadmap, not floating
- Adoption metrics are leading, not just lagging

**Produce:** Change Plan (intervention -> ADKAR stage -> audience -> owner -> date); Champion Network (named people per affected group); Adoption Metric Set

**Step output:** Change Plan

sections.heading: ADKAR in practice
sections.body:
| Stage | Question | Worked example |
|---|---|---|
| Awareness | Do they know why? | Grand-rounds briefing with Heads of Unit, not a memo |
| Desire | Do they want to? | Clinicians co-design the triage protocols |
| Knowledge | Do they know how? | Role-based training two weeks before R1 |
| Ability | Can they do it on the day? | Floor-walkers, GP liaison line, live referral-queue dashboard |
| Reinforcement | Will it stick? | Monthly champions call; measure in unit scorecards from R2 |

Most change plans are 80% Knowledge. Ask the agent: *"Audit my change plan by ADKAR stage. Which stage has the least activity for the highest-impact group?"*

**Try it in another industry.** *Government & NGOs:* run the ADKAR audit on a digital service redesign where frontline staff and community partners change in different releases. *Law Enforcement:* sequence a dispatch-optimisation roadmap where every release delivers standalone value without disrupting 24/7 operations.

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. Health information is sensitive information: never paste patient names, URNs, Medicare numbers, dates of birth, referral letters or clinical notes into any AI tool your organisation hasn't approved for it. The agent drafts; you own the decision.

sections.heading: Worked example — Outpatient access
sections.body:
*Instructor demo initiative: Shorter waits for specialist outpatient appointments (Riverside Health Network). Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation. No real patient data is used.*

**Delivery Roadmap.** R1 (weeks 1–12): e-referral MVP with submission validation and patient SMS acknowledgement in two pilot clinics (cardiology, orthopaedics) — standalone value: removes the fax-inbox wait and most returned referrals for pilot volume. R2 (weeks 13–20): daily protocol-led nurse triage + daily SMS appointment offers — standalone value: kills the biggest wait; depends on D2. R3 (weeks 21–30): roll-out to all 24 clinics. MVP defined; dependencies drawn; no release ships without its benefit measure live.

**Change Impact Assessment.** Triage clinicians (consultants and clinical nurse consultants) — high impact: new daily queue, protocol-led triage, changed measure; training + clinical supervision. Referral Hub and bookings admin — high: re-keying disappears, validation exceptions and SMS offers replace letters; role redesign and training. Outpatient call centre — medium: status calls deflect to SMS updates; scripts and dashboards change. GPs — medium: e-referral replaces fax; comms via the PHN and practice software vendors. Patients — low-to-positive: SMS updates; plain-language and translated guidance, with a phone option kept. Each group: what changes, magnitude, training, comms, measure.

**Change Plan.** ADKAR-mapped and sequenced ahead of each release. Awareness: grand-rounds briefing with Heads of Unit, not a memo. Desire: clinicians co-design the triage protocols; wait-time measure on unit dashboards. Knowledge: role-based training two weeks before R1. Ability: floor-walkers and a GP liaison line for the first fortnight, live referral-queue dashboard. Reinforcement: monthly champions call, measure in unit scorecards from R2. Adoption metrics: % e-referrals, clinician confidence pulse.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body:
**Delivery ships the solution. Change makes it stick.** Most change plans train people and forget Awareness, Desire and Reinforcement.

- Sequence releases that each deliver standalone value.
- Map change with ADKAR — skip a stage and adoption stalls.
- Diarise benefits reviews before go-live, not after.

**The questions that matter:** Who has to work differently, and do they know? What would make this not stick? How will we know the benefit actually landed?

**How a BA gathers the inputs:** Change-readiness conversations, capacity/planning workshop, impact interviews with affected groups, baseline measurement before go-live.

sections.heading: Playbook 06 · Step 4 — Define the Benefits Realisation Plan
sections.body:
**Inputs:** Approved Business Case, Delivery Roadmap, Change Plan

**What to do**
- Restate each benefit from the business case with its measurement method
- Set a baseline measurement before go-live for every benefit
- Define the cadence and owner for each post-go-live measurement
- Schedule a formal benefits review at 3, 6, and 12 months
- Define the corrective actions if benefits do not track to plan

**Success criteria**
- Every benefit has a baseline, owner, and measurement cadence
- Reviews are diarised before go-live, not after
- Corrective actions are pre-agreed, not invented under pressure

**Produce:** Benefits Realisation Plan (benefit -> measure -> baseline -> target -> owner -> cadence); Review Schedule (3 / 6 / 12 months); Corrective Action Playbook

**Step output:** Benefits Realisation Plan

Ask the agent: *"Trace each benefit back to a value leak and a business-case line. Flag any benefit with no owner, no baseline or no review date."*

**Try it in another industry.** *Logistics:* write a complete benefit definition for warehouse optimisation (measure, baseline, target, owner, cadence) with a WHS guardrail. *Higher Education:* define the guardrail for faster student-support response times — what harm would pushing the North Star too hard cause?

**AI guardrail.** Never paste confidential, commercial-in-confidence or personal information into a consumer AI tool. Use your organisation's enterprise or grounded version (Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team, Gemini for Workspace) or sanitise first: replace names with roles, round numbers, remove patient, client or customer identifiers, and use synthetic records for anything data-shaped. pathways.reference: Five Rovo agents, one BA: RA, SA, SM, TA and DOC agents, 14 automation rules, BA and PO gates, a real CI pipeline and zero self-approvals.
pathways.capstone: A Flow Blueprint: the status workflow with gates, agent roster and instructions, loop guard, traceability chain and rollout.
outcomes: Turn decision rights into status gates no agent can pass
Write agent instructions with strict outputs and guardrails
Keep REQ → story → test → evidence traceable and auditable
